extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply criteria about the nature, grounds, and limits of induction, deduction, demonstration, axioms, and definitions in the sciences and mathematics. Useful for evaluating claims about scientific method, mathematical necessity, and the epistemic status of axioms/definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as foundation of all sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: If, as laid down in the two preceding chapters, the foundation of all sciences, even deductive or demonstrative sciences, is Induction; if every step in the ratiocinations even of geometry is an act of induction; and if a train of reasoning is but bringing many inductions to bear upon the same subject of inquiry...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat all reasoning steps — including those in deductive sciences — as ultimately grounded in inductive generalizations. When evaluating a purportedly 'demonstrative' claim, check for underlying inductive premises. Example: geometrical reasoning depends on generalizations (definitions/axioms) drawn from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation from experimental to deductive via connecting inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: An experimental science transforms itself into a deductive science by the mere progress of experiment: a new set of instances, and a consequent new induction, may at any time bridge over the interval between two of these unconnected arches... some grand comprehensive induction may raise an arch high in the air, which bridges over hosts of them at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether new inductions connect previously detached generalizations; a single comprehensive induction (example: Newton's gravitation) can convert many empirical laws into deductively derivable consequences. Look for evidence that observed regularities have been shown to be uniformly consequent upon a better-known phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'marks' and chains of inference (marks of marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: We travel from a given visible or tangible fact, through the truths of numbers, to the fact sought. The given fact is a mark that a certain relation subsists between the quantities of some of the elements concerned; the one physical fact becomes a mark of the other, by being a mark of a mark of a mark of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inferring unobservables, require explicit chains of observable 'marks' linking to the inferred property. Evaluate the reliability of each link (direct observation vs. inferred) and the possibility that intermediate marks may be fallible or not perceptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as the chief agent for deductive extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand agent for transforming experimental into deductive sciences, is the science of number... if variations of quality correspond regularly to variations of quantity... every formula of mathematics applicable to quantities which vary in that particular manner, becomes a mark of a corresponding general truth respecting the variations in quality which accompany them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that mathematical formulation enables wide deductive reach only when qualitative phenomena correlate reliably with quantitative measures. Check that the assumed quantitative relations actually hold across the phenomena considered (examples: analytic geometry, mechanics, astronomy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions alone do not yield propositions without assuming corresponding real things
rubrics_metrics.description: From a definition as such, no proposition, unless it be one concerning the meaning of a word, can ever follow; and what apparently follows from a definition, follows in reality from an implied assumption that there exists a real thing conformable thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of treating definitions as sources of substantive truth. Require that definitions be linked to assumptions about real objects; evaluate whether such existence/possibility assumptions are warranted. Anti-pattern: treating purely verbal or conceptual definitions as establishing empirical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical definitions are hypothetical/approximate to real objects
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist no real things exactly conformable to the definitions of geometry... The points, lines, circles, and squares, which any one has in his mind, are (I apprehend) simply copies of the points, lines, circles, and squares which he has known in his experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying geometrical results to physical objects, note that the idealized definitions are approximations. Evaluate whether the approximation error is negligible for practical purposes; if not, require correction terms or supplementary propositions addressing the 'aberration' (e.g., line breadth, thermal expansion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms differ from definitions; axioms are generalizations from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: They are experimental truths; generalizations from observation. The proposition, Two straight lines cannot inclose a space ... is an induction from the evidence of our senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat axioms as empirically grounded generalizations rather than purely apriori truths. When judging axioms, look for their observational basis and the extent of confirmatory experience. Be cautious about claiming purely mental intuition as the sole ground for axiomatic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical necessity is conditional on hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity ascribed to the truths of mathematics ... is an illusion; the conclusions of geometry are necessary only in this, that they necessarily follow from the suppositions from which they are deduced. Those suppositions ... are not even true; they purposely depart, more or less widely, from the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims of 'necessary' or 'necessary truth' as conditional necessity relative to the adopted hypotheses. Evaluate whether the hypotheses themselves are true/appropriate for the domain; the force of mathematical demonstration depends on the relevance and truth of initial assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses for scientific inquiry must relate to real objects and avoid ascribing false properties
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis framed for the purpose of scientific inquiry must relate to something which has real existence... we must not ascribe to the thing any property which it has not; our liberty extends only to suppressing some of those which it has, under the indispensable obligation of restoring them whenever... their presence or absence would make any material difference in the truth of our conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that hypotheses be realistic approximations: allowed simplifications must not introduce false properties. Check that when simplifications are used, the investigator accounts for when and how to restore omitted properties if they materially affect conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct approximations by adding propositions about aberrations when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When we have occasion to extend these inductions, or their consequences, to cases in which the error would be appreciable... we correct our conclusions, by combining with them a fresh set of propositions relating to the aberration; just as we also take in propositions relating to the physical or chemical properties of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications beyond the idealized domain, demand explicit corrective propositions describing deviations and how they modify results. Example: include material properties (thermal expansion) when geometry alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of irreducible axioms (some fundamental truths are indemonstrable)
rubrics_metrics.description: There will be found in the list of axioms two or three fundamental truths, not capable of being demonstrated: among which I agree with Mr. Whewell in placing the proposition that two straight lines cannot inclose a space ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that some foundational propositions must be accepted without proof (indemonstrable axioms). When evaluating a system, identify such irreducible principles and assess their empirical standing or necessity for the deductive structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical confirmation strengthens axioms even if argued apriori
rubrics_metrics.description: They cannot, however, but allow that the truth of the axiom... is also evident from experience. Whether the axiom needs confirmation or not, it receives confirmation in almost every instant of our lives; Experimental proof crowds in upon us in such endless profusion...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when an axiom is defended on apriori grounds, check for abundant experiential confirmation. Use the degree and ubiquity of empirical corroboration as a measure of the axiom's reliability for practical reasoning.
